settings.heading: No trace amounts.
settings.text: Most hair oils put just enough of a “hero” ingredient on the label to tell a good story — not enough to actually work. Here’s exactly what’s in Kehsora, and why each one earned its place.

settings.name: Rosemary
settings.text:
Rosemary has been used for centuries — not just in cooking, but as a remedy for scalp health across the Mediterranean and in Ayurveda alike. It works by improving blood circulation to the scalp, meaning hair follicles receive more of what they need to actually grow stronger.

It also carries natural antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory properties, calming an irritated or flaky scalp along the way.
settings.benefits: Scalp circulation, Follicle strength, Calms irritation
settings.best_for: Thinning, slow growth, flaky or itchy scalp
settings.pairs: Bhringraj for hair fall · Peppermint for growth
settings.science:
Rosemary is the best-studied hair herb outside Ayurveda. In a 2015 randomised trial, 100 adults with pattern hair loss used either rosemary oil or 2% minoxidil for six months (Panahi et al., SKINmed). Both groups had a similar increase in hair count by month six, and the rosemary group reported less scalp itching.

Its carnosic and rosmarinic acids are strong antioxidants and calm inflammation on the scalp. The trial also shows why patience matters: little changed at three months, and the difference showed at six.
settings.how_to_use:
Blend: mix 1 part concentrate with 5 parts of your base oil — 30ml into 150ml, or 50ml into 250ml. Shake before each use.

Apply: part your hair and massage a few drops into the scalp with your fingertips for 3–5 minutes. Leave on for at least 30 minutes, or overnight, then wash.

How often: 2–3 times a week. Give it 6–12 weeks — hair grows slowly, and so do results.

Tip: rosemary is one of our most stimulating concentrates — you may feel a gentle warmth or tingle. That's normal; if it stings, blend it more dilute.

Patch-test on the inside of your arm 24 hours before first use, and keep away from the eyes.

settings.name: Bhringraj
settings.text:
Bhringraj literally translates to “ruler of hair” in Sanskrit — a name it’s carried in classical Ayurvedic texts for thousands of years, long before “hair growth serums” existed. It’s known to stimulate hair follicles and improve scalp circulation, supporting stronger roots and reduced hair fall over time.

It’s also traditionally used to slow premature greying, and its natural cooling properties help with an overheated, stressed scalp.
settings.benefits: Reduces hair fall, Strengthens roots, Cooling & calming
settings.origin: Grows wild in damp ground across India
settings.preparation: Slow heat-infused into oil, the traditional Ayurvedic way
settings.best_for: Hair fall, weak roots, early greying, an overheated scalp
settings.pairs: Rosemary for growth · Lavender to soothe
settings.science:
Bhringraj — also called Keshraj, “king of hair” — appears throughout classical Ayurveda as the herb for hair and scalp. Traditionally it is cooked slowly into oil so its active compounds pass into the oil.

Modern research is early but encouraging. In a 2008 study, an Eclipta alba extract applied to the skin of rats moved hair follicles into the growth phase sooner than in untreated rats, and did better than 2% minoxidil in that test (Roy et al., Archives of Dermatological Research). Human trials are still limited, so we see it as a time-tested herb with promising science behind it — not a miracle cure.
settings.how_to_use:
Blend: mix 1 part concentrate with 5 parts of your base oil — 30ml into 150ml, or 50ml into 250ml. Shake before each use.

Apply: part your hair and massage a few drops into the scalp with your fingertips for 3–5 minutes. Leave on for at least 30 minutes, or overnight, then wash.

How often: 2–3 times a week. Give it 6–12 weeks — hair grows slowly, and so do results.

Tip: Bhringraj is cooling, which is why it is traditionally used at night. Massage it in before bed and wash in the morning.

Patch-test on the inside of your arm 24 hours before first use, and keep away from the eyes.

settings.name: Jojoba
settings.text:
Jojoba closely mimics your scalp’s own natural sebum, which means it absorbs rather than sits heavy on top — ideal for an oily scalp or anyone who finds traditional oils too greasy to use regularly. It’s naturally lightweight and non-comedogenic.

Gentle enough for daily use, blended into a heavier base oil it lightens the whole mix for a fast-absorbing, non-greasy finish — and it’s just as kind to the skin, softening dry patches without clogging pores.

On the lengths, it coats and smooths each strand like a light serum — sealing in moisture for glossier, less frizzy hair.
settings.benefits: Lightweight, Balances oily scalp, Shine & less frizz
settings.origin: A desert shrub of the Sonoran Desert (Mexico and the south-western US)
settings.best_for: Oily or dandruff-prone scalps, frizzy or dull hair, daily use, anyone who finds oils heavy
settings.pairs: Rosemary for growth · Bhringraj for hair fall
settings.science:
Jojoba isn't really an oil at all — it's a liquid wax, made of long-chain wax esters that are remarkably similar to the wax esters in your own sebum. That likeness is why it spreads easily and sinks in instead of sitting on top.

Being a wax, it is also very stable and slow to go rancid. It rates low on comedogenic scales, so it is gentle on scalps prone to build-up, and it helps skin hold moisture without feeling greasy.
settings.how_to_use:
Blend: mix 1 part concentrate with 5 parts of your base oil — 30ml into 150ml, or 50ml into 250ml. Shake before each use.

Apply: part your hair and massage a few drops into the scalp with your fingertips for 3–5 minutes. Leave on for at least 30 minutes, or overnight, then wash.

How often: 2–3 times a week. Give it 6–12 weeks — hair grows slowly, and so do results.

Tip: because it absorbs so well, jojoba works as a light leave-in too — warm one or two drops between your palms and smooth over dry ends.

Patch-test on the inside of your arm 24 hours before first use, and keep away from the eyes.

settings.name: Peppermint
settings.text:
Peppermint is the cooling one. Its menthol gives that instant fresh tingle on the scalp — and that sensation comes with increased blood flow to the skin, which is exactly what sleepy follicles need.

It also clears and refreshes an oily or heavy-feeling scalp, so it’s a favourite for anyone who wants their oiling ritual to feel invigorating rather than greasy.
settings.benefits: Wakes up the scalp, Supports growth, Cooling, refreshing
settings.origin: A natural cross of watermint and spearmint; India is one of the world’s largest mint growers
settings.best_for: Thinning, slow growth, oily or dull-feeling scalp
settings.pairs: Rosemary for circulation · Cedarwood for thinning
settings.science:
In a 2014 study (Oh et al., Toxicological Research), 3% peppermint oil applied to the skin of mice for four weeks produced more hair follicles, deeper follicles and a thicker dermal layer than the control groups — with results on par with or ahead of 3% minoxidil, and no signs of toxicity.

It’s an animal study, so we don’t promise miracles — but it fits what menthol is known to do: it increases blood flow to the skin where it’s applied, bringing more nutrients to the follicle.
settings.how_to_use:
Blend: mix 1 part concentrate with 5 parts of your base oil — 30ml into 150ml, or 50ml into 250ml. Shake before each use.

Apply: part your hair and massage a few drops of the blend into the scalp with your fingertips for 3–5 minutes. Leave on for at least 30 minutes, or overnight, then wash.

How often: 2–3 times a week. Give it 6–12 weeks — hair grows slowly, and so do results.

Tip: the cool tingle is normal and fades in a few minutes. If it feels too strong, use more base oil in your blend.

Keep well away from the eyes, and wash your hands after applying. Not for children under 6 — and never near a young child’s face or nose. Patch-test 24 hours before first use.

settings.name: Tea Tree
settings.text:
Tea tree is the scalp’s deep-cleaner. It’s naturally antibacterial and antifungal, which makes it the go-to for dandruff, itchy flakes and the greasy build-up that clogs the follicle.

A clean, calm scalp is the foundation for healthy hair — so tea tree clears the ground for everything else in your ritual to work.
settings.benefits: Fights flakes, Clears build-up, Calms itch
settings.origin: Native to New South Wales, Australia
settings.best_for: Dandruff, itchy or flaky scalp, oily build-up
settings.pairs: Jojoba to clear build-up · Lavender to calm itch
settings.science:
Tea tree is one of the most researched essential oils. Its main active, terpinen-4-ol, has well-documented antibacterial, antifungal and anti-inflammatory activity (Carson et al., Clinical Microbiology Reviews, 2006).

In a randomised trial of 126 people with dandruff, a 5% tea tree oil shampoo used daily for four weeks improved dandruff severity by 41%, against 11% for placebo — with less itching and greasiness, and no side effects reported (Satchell et al., Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology, 2002).
settings.how_to_use:
Blend: mix 1 part concentrate with 5 parts of your base oil — 30ml into 150ml, or 50ml into 250ml. Shake before each use.

Apply: part your hair and massage a few drops of the blend into the scalp with your fingertips for 3–5 minutes. Leave on for at least 30 minutes, or overnight, then wash.

How often: 2–3 times a week. Give it 6–12 weeks — hair grows slowly, and so do results.

Tip: for stubborn flakes, leave the blend on for an hour before washing, 2–3 times a week.

Never swallow — tea tree oil is harmful if ingested — and keep it away from pets, especially cats. Keep away from the eyes, and patch-test 24 hours before first use.

settings.name: Lavender
settings.text:
Lavender is the gentle one. It soothes an itchy, sensitive or irritated scalp, has natural antimicrobial properties, and its scent is one of the most relaxing in aromatherapy — which turns your oiling ritual into a real wind-down.

Stress is one of the quiet causes of hair fall, so an evening ritual that actually calms you is part of the point.
settings.benefits: Soothes irritation, Supports growth, Calming aroma
settings.origin: Native to the Mediterranean; grown across Europe and the Himalayan foothills
settings.best_for: Itchy or sensitive scalp, stress-related shedding, evening ritual
settings.pairs: Tea Tree for itchy flakes · Cedarwood for thinning
settings.science:
In a 2016 study (Lee et al., Toxicological Research), 3% and 5% lavender oil applied to mice for four weeks significantly increased the number and depth of hair follicles and thickened the skin layer that supports them.

Lavender was also one of the four oils in a well-known randomised trial for alopecia areata (Hay et al., Archives of Dermatology, 1998), where a daily scalp massage with the essential-oil blend helped 44% of people, against 15% with carrier oil alone.
settings.how_to_use:
Blend: mix 1 part concentrate with 5 parts of your base oil — 30ml into 150ml, or 50ml into 250ml. Shake before each use.

Apply: part your hair and massage a few drops of the blend into the scalp with your fingertips for 3–5 minutes. Leave on for at least 30 minutes, or overnight, then wash.

How often: 2–3 times a week. Give it 6–12 weeks — hair grows slowly, and so do results.

Tip: lavender is the gentlest of our concentrates and the perfect evening oil — massage it in before bed and wash out in the morning.

Keep away from the eyes and patch-test 24 hours before first use. Pregnant or breastfeeding? Check with your doctor first.

settings.name: Cedarwood
settings.text:
Cedarwood brings a warm, woody depth to your ritual. It has traditionally been used to balance an oily scalp and keep flaking in check, and it’s one of the classic oils in scalp massages for thinning hair.

Its grounding, calming aroma also makes it a lovely partner to lavender for an evening ritual.
settings.benefits: Supports thicker hair, Balances the scalp, Grounding aroma
settings.botanical: Cedrus atlantica / Cedrus deodara (Atlas or Himalayan cedar)
settings.origin: Atlas cedar grows in the mountains of Morocco; Himalayan cedar (deodar) is native to India
settings.best_for: Thinning or patchy hair, oily scalp, grounding evening ritual
settings.pairs: Peppermint for growth · Lavender to calm
settings.science:
Cedarwood was one of the four essential oils — with thyme, rosemary and lavender — in a randomised, double-blind trial of 86 people with alopecia areata (Hay et al., Archives of Dermatology, 1998). After seven months of daily scalp massage, 44% of the essential-oil group improved, against 15% of those using only the carrier oils.

In the lab, cedar oil also shows strong antibacterial and antifungal activity (Molecules, 2023), which supports its traditional use for a flaky, oily scalp.
settings.how_to_use:
Blend: mix 1 part concentrate with 5 parts of your base oil — 30ml into 150ml, or 50ml into 250ml. Shake before each use.

Apply: part your hair and massage a few drops of the blend into the scalp with your fingertips for 3–5 minutes. Leave on for at least 30 minutes, or overnight, then wash.

How often: 2–3 times a week. Give it 6–12 weeks — hair grows slowly, and so do results.

Tip: cedarwood works best as part of a long, slow scalp massage — take your time with it.

Keep away from the eyes and patch-test 24 hours before first use. Pregnant or breastfeeding? Check with your doctor first.

settings.heading: Formulated with purpose,
settings.text: Every generic oil on the market is a broad-spectrum guess. Kehsora is built the opposite way — real, potent ingredients, chosen for exactly what they do, infused properly rather than diluted for a label.
